name: Atikamekw
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Beland, Jean-Pierre. 1978. Atikamekw Morphology and Lexicon. PhD thesis, University of California, Berkeley.

new_statements.quote: Short /i/, /a/ and /o/ are subject to a certain number of phonemic rules that sometimes neutralize completely their vowel quality. In weak (unstressed) syllables, short vowels are indiscriminantely centralized to -ʌ- or -ə-; e.g., the vowels /o/ in a:šokan 'bridge, pier, wharf' and /i/ in ašikan 'stockings' are phonetically identical. [...] In absolute final position, short vowels are usually deleted in polysyllabic words; e.g., /amiskwa/, amiskw 'beaver'. Exceptions are found, however, and not only in monosyllabic words; when occuring in this position, short vowels usually receive a secondary stress. E.g., niska 'goose'; maskwa 'bear'; mikko 'blood'; otehi 'heart'.
new_statements.citation: Béland, Jean Pierre. 1978. Atikamekw Morphology and Lexicon. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Berkeley (Ann Arbor: UMI). §12.5.08 Vowels, p. 302.
new_statements.locator: §12.5.08 'Vowels', dissertation p. 302 (= PDF page 320 of the eScholarship scan)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Béland recognises stressed ('strong') versus weak/unstressed syllables (short vowels centralise to [ʌ]/[ə] in unstressed syllables) and says a short vowel that survives in absolute word-final position usually carries a secondary stress; he never states where primary word stress falls. The examples (niska, maskwa, mikko, otehi with final secondary stress) are consistent with non-final primary stress but the source does not say so. No placement rule can be read off this source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicit: retained word-final short vowels 'usually receive a secondary stress' (niska 'goose', maskwa 'bear', mikko 'blood', otehi 'heart').
new_statements.exceptions: None about primary stress (none stated). Final short vowels are usually deleted in polysyllables (amiskw 'beaver') but kept in many particles (ekoši 'let's go', ni:šitana 'twenty').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonemics of vowels in citation-form words); data from the three Atikamekw communities Manouane, Weymontachie, Obedjiwan, 1974-77. No mention of phrase-level accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Béland 1978 describes 'Atikamekw, a Cree dialect' of Manouane, Weymontachie and Obedjiwan (all three communities, 1974-77 fieldwork) = atik1240 as a whole; he notes Obedjiwan /r/~/l/ variation but treats one language. Cooper 1945 'Tête-de-Boule Cree' is the same language under its older exonym (Weymontachingue-area speakers).

sources.citation: Junker, Marie-Odile & Nicole Petiquay (co-dirs.), with Véronique Chachai. 2019-2023. Orthographe / Grammaire atikamekw. langueatikamekw.ca (Carleton University / Conseil de la Nation Atikamekw); orthography page cites Institut Linguistique Atikamekw (ILA). 1997. Guide orthographique de la langue atikamekw. La Tuque.
sources.note: Orthography page: a/i/o each represent a long and a short vowel, e always long; fortis/lenis not written; nothing on stress or accent. Grammar pages (noms, verbes, reduplication etc.) are morphological; no stress statement.
